outputs.L1:
The body of the boy who took his flight  
off the cliff at Kilcloher into the sea  
was hauled up by curragh-men, out at first light  
fishing for mackerel in the estuary.  

“No requiem or rosary,” said the priest,  
“nor consecrated ground for burial,”  
as if the boy had flown beyond the pale  
of mercy, redemption, or God’s love.  

“Forgive them, for they know not what they do,”  
quoth Argyle to the dead boy’s people,  
who heard in what he said a kind of riddle,  
as if he meant their coreligionists  
and not their sodden, sadly broken boy.  

Either way, they took some comfort in it  
and prepared better than accustomed fare  
of food and spirits, by their own reckoning:  
the greater the sin, the greater the toll.  

But Argyle refused their shilling coin  
and helped them build a box and dig a grave.  
“Your boy’s no profligate or prodigal,”  
he said, “only a wounded pilgrim, like us all.  
What say his leaping was a leap of faith  
into his father’s beckoning embrace?”  

They killed no fatted calf. They filled the hole.
outputs.L2:
At daybreak, curragh fishermen searching for mackerel in the estuary recovered the body of a boy who had hurled himself from the cliffs of Kilcloher into the sea.

The priest denied him funeral prayers and refused him a grave in blessed earth, speaking as though the boy’s death had carried him beyond compassion, salvation, and divine love. Argyle urged the grieving family to pardon those responsible, since they did not understand their actions. His words puzzled them: they thought he might be referring to others of their faith rather than to their drenched and shattered son.

Still, the family drew some solace from what he said. They prepared more food and drink than they ordinarily would have offered, reasoning that a graver transgression demanded a higher payment. Argyle, however, would not accept their shilling. Instead, he helped them make a coffin and excavate a burial place.

He told them their son had been neither dissolute nor wayward, but merely another injured traveler through life, no different from the rest of humanity. Perhaps, he suggested, the boy’s plunge could be understood as an act of trust—a jump into the open arms of his waiting father.

No celebratory calf was slaughtered. They simply covered the grave.
outputs.L3:
Curragh fishermen recover the body of a boy who has leapt from the cliffs at Kilcloher into the sea. His devastated family seeks the customary rites of mourning, but the priest refuses to grant him a requiem, a rosary, or burial in consecrated ground because his death is judged to be suicide.

In the midst of this rejection, Argyle offers the family the compassion they have been denied. His scriptural language initially confuses them, but his actions make his sympathy clear. He refuses any payment, helps to build the boy’s coffin, and assists in digging the grave. Rather than condemning the dead boy as a sinner, Argyle describes him as a wounded pilgrim—a suffering soul whose final act should be met with mercy rather than judgment.

The boy is ultimately buried without religious ceremony. Yet Argyle gives the family a more consoling way to understand his death: perhaps the boy’s leap was not simply a fall into despair, but a leap into his father’s waiting embrace. Through this image, Argyle transforms an act surrounded by shame and exclusion into one that may still contain the possibility of forgiveness, love, and spiritual homecoming.
outputs.L4:
The poem tells the tragic story of a boy who dies by suicide and of the conflict that follows over how he should be remembered and buried. Because the Church regards his death as a grave sin, the priest refuses to grant him sacred rites or allow the usual forms of religious consolation. This denial adds another layer of pain to the family’s grief: they must mourn not only the loss of the boy, but also the judgment imposed on him after death.

Against the priest’s rigid condemnation stands Argyle, whose response is shaped by compassion rather than doctrine. He helps the family bury the boy and speaks of him without accusation or shame. Instead of reducing the boy to the manner of his death, Argyle recognizes his suffering and preserves his dignity. His words challenge the idea that a single desperate act can define an entire life.

Argyle therefore reimagines the boy not as an unforgivable sinner, but as a wounded pilgrim overwhelmed by pain. He describes the death as a kind of leap of faith: uncertain and tragic, yet still directed toward the possibility of peace, understanding, or mercy. The image does not erase the sorrow of what happened, but it offers the grieving family a gentler way to understand it.

Through the contrast between the priest and Argyle, the poem questions religious judgment when it is separated from human sympathy. The priest represents rules, exclusion, and condemnation, while Argyle embodies kindness, practical care, and spiritual generosity. His willingness to help with the burial turns compassion itself into a sacred act. Ultimately, the poem suggests that mercy may extend beyond the boundaries of doctrine and that the boy’s suffering deserves understanding rather than rejection.
outputs.L5:
## The God of Kilcloher

In Kilcloher, where the wind moves softly across the fields and the rain darkens the old stone walls, people once spoke of God as though He lived nearby. They found Him in the silence before dawn, in the cry of birds above the hills, and in the warm light shining from cottage windows.

The God of Kilcloher was not distant or hidden beyond the clouds. He walked beside those who laboured, comforted those who mourned, and listened to prayers whispered along lonely roads. His presence was felt in simple kindness: a neighbour sharing bread, a stranger offered shelter, or a family gathering beside the fire.

Though times changed and many old stories faded, Kilcloher kept its quiet sense of the sacred. The fields, stones, and open sky still seemed to carry a promise—that even in the smallest and most forgotten places, God could be found.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a narrative poem set in rural Ireland about a boy who dies by suicide after jumping from a cliff, is denied a Catholic burial, and is ultimately buried with compassion by a man named Argyle.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Field Beyond the Wall**

In a rain-bit parish west of Clare,  
where stone walls stitched the bog to sea,  
a boy named Eamon minded sheep  
and whistled blackbirds from the tree.

His father’s hands were hard with turf,  
his mother’s rosary worn white;  
the chapel bell divided days,  
the Atlantic troubled every night.

What sorrow grew inside the lad  
no neighbour knew, no priest could tell.  
He bore it like a hidden thorn  
beneath the tongue, beneath the bell.

One dusk, when gannets crossed the gale  
and clouds lay low on Moher’s crown,  
he walked the path above the foam  
and, lost to hope, went falling down.

The sea returned him with the dawn  
among the wrack below the height.  
His mother knelt beside his coat  
and called him home till morning’s light.

But Father Byrne stood at the gate,  
his book held closed against his breast:  
“No hallowed ground,” the canon said,  
“may take the soul that spurned its rest.”

The village lowered every face.  
No hand was raised, no answer made.  
The rain went ticking on the stones;  
the mother trembled where she prayed.

Then Argyle came from Ballymore,  
a widowed man with silver hair,  
who shod the horses, mended ploughs,  
and kept few words, but kept them fair.

“I’ll dig,” he said. “The Lord who made  
that frightened child knows more than we.  
No law of ours can sound the dark  
that drove him to the cliff and sea.”

Beyond the wall, in nettled earth,  
where hawthorn leaned across the sod,  
he worked beneath the winter rain  
and left the judgement all to God.

He lined the grave with rush and fern,  
then laid the young boy gently down;  
the mother placed a rowan sprig,  
the father set his only crown—

a cap the lad had worn to fairs,  
still smelling faintly of the peat.  
And Argyle filled the grave by hand,  
each spadeful sorrowful and sweet.

No bell was rung, no Latin said,  
no candle lit the chapel nave;  
yet curlews cried above the field,  
and wild thyme gathered at the grave.

By spring, the children passing there  
would stop beside the hawthorn tree,  
and leave small shells and primrose heads  
brought shining from the western sea.

Years later, when the wall fell down  
and rules grew kinder than before,  
they moved no bone, disturbed no stone,  
but made a pathway from the door.

And on the gate they fixed a cross,  
plain oak, without a saint or name,  
save these few words that Argyle spoke  
when fear had hardened into blame:

**No soul is saved by casting out,  
nor grief made clean by rigid art.  
Where earth denies a place to rest,  
let mercy make the ground a heart.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dark, lyrical poem in loose blank verse about fishermen recovering a drowned boy, a priest refusing him a requiem, and an outsider who reframes the boy’s fatal leap as a wounded pilgrim’s leap of faith.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn the nets came burdened to the quay,  
not silver with the weather of the shoals,  
but bowed around a boy the tide had kept  
all night beneath its cold, unanswering tongue.

The fishermen drew off their woolen caps.  
They knew his hands, the scar above his brow,  
the boots his mother mended every spring.  
We lift what the black water gives, one said,  
and no one dared to name what it had taken.

They bore him through the village on a sail,  
while gulls wheeled like torn pages overhead.  
The chapel bell remained a fist of iron.  
The priest stood in the doorway, pale and straight,  
his book shut hard against the dripping dead.

No requiem for one who chose the deep.  
No candle for the soul that broke its vessel.  
The earth itself, he said, must turn its face.

Then from the road a stranger left the rain,  
a woman with a thornwood staff, whose coat  
was patched with maps and dust from other griefs.  
She knelt beside the boy and touched his hair  
as if to wake a pilgrim at a shrine.

You call it choice, she said. I call it wound.  
You call the cliff an altar to despair;  
perhaps he saw, beyond our blinded shore,  
one farther lamp, and leapt because he thought  
the dark was only distance from its flame.

Not every faith arrives on bended knee.  
Some faith is fever, cornered, without speech;  
some faith mistakes the abyss for open arms.  
The leap was not made holy by the fall,  
nor was it sin because the sea was strong.

She took the priest’s closed book into her hands  
and laid it, still unopened, on his breast.  
The fishermen began a low, rough hymn,  
each voice a rope cast out too late, yet cast.

And when they dug his grave beyond the wall,  
where nettles drank the salt wind from the stones,  
the stranger faced the unrelenting sea:

Receive no praise for keeping what you keep.  
Return no blame upon the broken-hearted.  
This boy came to your edge a wounded pilgrim,  
and if he leapt, he leapt toward something bright—  
though none of us could see it through the storm.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a historically flavored Irish poem that explores religious intolerance toward suicide. Include curragh-men fishing for mackerel, the phrase “Forgive them, for they know not what they do,” and allusions to the prodigal son.
counterfactuals.output:
### **Beyond the Churchyard Wall**

At dawn the curragh-men pulled out,  
black ribs upon the pewter bay,  
to fish for mackerel, quick as coins  
beneath the cold, reluctant day.  

Behind them, under hawthorn shade,  
the chapel bell refused to toll;  
the priest had barred the eastern gate  
against a self-forsaken soul.  

“No Christian clay,” the elders said,  
“may hold the hand that broke God’s thread.”  
So neighbours dug beyond the wall,  
where nettles kept the nameless dead.  

His mother came with Sunday bread,  
though none would meet her mourning eyes;  
she whispered, “Once a son came home,  
and love ran forth before replies.  

“Was there no robe, no ring, no feast  
for one who lost the road in pain?  
Must Heaven’s door be bolted fast  
because he could not knock again?”  

The mackerel flashed in woven nets;  
the curraghs leaned against the foam.  
Each silver body, sea-returned,  
shone like a prodigal come home.  

Then through the salt wind rose her prayer,  
more fierce than sermon, law, or feud:  
“Forgive them, for they know not what they do,”  
and kissed the unconsecrated dew.  

That night, beyond the churchyard wall,  
the hawthorn flowered, pale and wild;  
and God—who knew the farthest road—  
went out to meet His banished child.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a tragic poem set at Kilcloher in which a bereaved family prepares customary food, drink, and payment after their son’s body is pulled from the sea, but a compassionate figure called Argyle refuses the coin and helps dig the grave.
counterfactuals.output:
### **At Kilcloher**

At Kilcloher the sea gave back  
what it had taken in the squall—  
their youngest son, with weed in his hair  
and salt upon him like a pall.

They laid him where the fire burned low,  
beneath the clock’s unanswering chime;  
his mother washed his hands with milk,  
as she had done in cradle-time.

His sisters kneaded mourning bread,  
his father poured the whiskey round;  
they set the cold meat by the hearth  
for those who’d bear him to the ground.

And by the door, beneath a cloth,  
the customary coin was laid—  
a poor man’s silver, scraped and saved,  
the last small debt that grief could pay.

But Argyle came before the dawn  
and saw the father stooped and grey.  
He closed the dead boy’s sea-blind eyes  
and pushed the offered coin away.

“No gold could make this burden light,  
nor silver buy him rest,” he said;  
then took a spade to Kilcloher hill  
and broke the bitter earth instead.

All morning long the rain came down,  
the black sea struck the cliffs below;  
and Argyle dug beside the kin  
where thorn and bent grass leaned with woe.

They drank one cup beside the grave  
and left the bread upon a stone.  
The tide went out from Kilcloher—  
the grieving family walked home alone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a restrained, emotionally powerful narrative poem about mercy versus church doctrine: a priest denies consecrated ground to a drowned suicide, while another man comforts the family, builds the coffin, and suggests the death might be understood as a return to the father’s embrace.
counterfactuals.output:
### Outside the Wall

They brought him up at morning,  
riverweed wound through his hands,  
his coat made heavy with water,  
his face emptied of weather.

The priest came late. He stood  
beneath the dripping yews  
and would not cross the threshold  
where the mother knelt.

“No bell,” he said. “No blessing.  
The law is plain.”  
Behind him, the churchyard grass  
shone with rain.

So they carried the drowned man  
beyond the wall,  
where nettles kept no doctrine  
and stones had no names.

One man stayed.

He sat beside the father  
until the lamp burned low,  
then planed six boards smooth  
and fitted them without speech.

At dawn he brought the coffin,  
pale wood, clean nails.  
He washed the mud from the dead man’s feet  
and covered them with linen.

The mother asked where mercy lived  
if not beneath the cross.

The man looked toward the river,  
then toward her empty arms.

“Perhaps,” he said, “the water  
was not a gate he closed,  
but the last dark field he crossed  
before his father found him.

“Perhaps he could not see the road.  
Perhaps he only heard  
someone calling from the far bank  
in a voice he knew.”

They buried him outside the wall.  
No bell spoke. No priest.

But the father lowered the coffin  
as gently as a child,  
and the mother cast in flowers  
the church had never blessed.

All night the rain fell evenly  
on grave and consecrated ground.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
